notes.body:
The Quran here reaches back to something the passage carefully calls not just a moment but 'a degree of being' — and that phrase unlocks the whole puzzle. When we hear the word *moment*, we picture a dot on a calendar, a single tick of the clock that came and went. But the covenant (میثاق) of 'Am I not your Lord?' does not live on the calendar at all, because the calendar belongs to the physical world, and this reality stands before that world and above it.

> أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ ۖ قَالُوا۟ بَلَىٰ ۛ شَهِدْنَآ
>
> 'Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, verily, we testify.'
>
> Al-A'raf 7:172

So how can one moment be both a real event and an ever-present truth inside us right now? It helps to hear two meanings in the word *when*. There is the clock-when of dates and hours, and there is a deeper when — a layer, a depth, the way a foundation sits beneath every room of a house at once. The covenant's when is that second kind: real, and prior to us, the way the foundation is under the very floor we stand on this second.

Picture a wax seal. The signet is pressed into the wax one time, in a single act; yet the impression it leaves stays present continuously, shaping the wax ever after. Our soul is that wax. The pressing was the covenant; the shape it left is the conscience (ضمیر) that stirs in us whenever we feel the difference between right and wrong. **Every pang of conscience is that same covenant speaking again in the present tense.**

That is why the passage says the moment 'enters into the very shaping of the human soul.' It is not a faded memory we strain to recall from long ago — it is the ground we stand on. And Allah made every soul witness it, شَهِدْنَا, so that not one of us could ever honestly claim we never knew our Lord.

etymology: میثاق (covenant): from the root و-ث-ق, to bind firmly and to trust. The same root gives وثیق, firm and secure, and ثقۃ, trust. A میثاق is no casual word but a bond tied tight — a pact fastened so securely it cannot slip loose.

ذُرّیّۃ (progeny): from the root ذ-ر-ر, meaning tiny scattered particles, like specks of dust in a shaft of light. The seed drawn from the children of Adam is pictured as countless minute souls, each a single particle carrying the whole covenant within it.

شَهِدْنَا (we testify): from the root ش-ه-د, to be present and to witness. To witness is first of all to be there; the soul's answering 'Yes, we testify' means it stood present at its own making and can never plead that it was absent.

notes.body:
*Researched outside this library — the knowledge base carries nothing on this passage. Sources are listed at the end.*

The single chapter of the Quran that does not open with the phrase 'the infinitely Compassionate, the ever-Merciful' (بِسْمِ ٱللَّٰهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ) is the ninth one, At-Tawbah, which is also known as Bara’ah (براءة), or 'The Release'. This exception is understood to be deeply connected to the chapter's specific historical context and subject matter, which includes a declaration of disavowal from treaties with certain groups who had repeatedly violated their agreements.

This omission does not weaken the principle that mercy takes precedence over wrath; rather, it highlights the gravity of the situation being addressed. The Bismillah, as the opening phrase is known, is seen as a declaration of safety and mercy. Its absence at the beginning of At-Tawbah signals that the chapter opens not with an offer of peace, but with a stern ultimatum and a warning. Maulana Ali is reported to have explained that the Bismillah signifies security (أمان), whereas this chapter was revealed in a context of conflict and the breaking of covenants.

However, the theme of mercy is not absent from the chapter. In fact, the chapter's very name, At-Tawbah, means 'The Repentance,' pointing directly toward the path of return to Allah's mercy. Even within its stern verses, the chapter offers protection and forgiveness to those who cease their hostility and turn towards repentance. The omission is therefore a specific rhetorical and contextual choice for this one chapter, while the foundational principle of divine reality, stated in a sacred tradition (hadith qudsi), remains that 'My mercy takes precedence over My wrath'. The other 113 chapters begin with the Bismillah, reinforcing mercy as the overwhelming norm and the essential nature of the Divine.

***

**Etymology**

براءة (release): From the root ب-ر-ء, which means to be free from, to be clear of, or to be healed. The word براءة signifies a declaration of being free and clear from an obligation or a treaty. It is a formal disavowal, an announcement that a previous connection or agreement is now void, hence the English rendering 'release' or 'immunity'.

أمان (security): From the root أ-م-ن, which carries the core meaning of safety, security, and trustworthiness. This root gives rise to words like إيمان (faith), which is to place one's trust in Allah and feel secure in that belief. The word أمان itself denotes a guarantee of safety, a pledge of protection, or a state of being secure from harm.

notes.body:
Reality here is not a switch that is simply on or off — it comes in degrees, like light. Two souls can both exist and yet not be equally *filled* with being; one can carry more of what is truly real than the other. **The measure of that fullness is nearness to الحق, the Real — the ground from which everything else borrows its existence.**

الحق lends being to all things, and its innermost character is mercy, not wrath. This is the whole force of the divine saying that mercy takes precedence over wrath. Mercy is not one quality among many — it is **the very grain of ultimate reality**, while wrath, punishment and severity belong to the passing, relative side of things, real only in a borrowed and lesser way.

That gives us the answer. A soul grows more real the more it lets the Real shine through it, and it does that by reflecting mercy. Think of the soul as a mirror:

- A clean mirror throws back nearly all the light that falls on it.
- A clouded, dusty mirror throws back only a little.
- Both are mirrors, yet one carries far more of the light it was made to hold.

The merciful soul is the clean mirror. Wrath and hardness are the dust — real enough as smudges, but they dim the reflection and pull the soul toward the thin, fading edge of being.

So when the passage calls one soul 'more real' than another, it is not weighing how much each exists but how much of الحق lives in them. A soul that forgives, that pours out رحمة, is turned toward the deepest and most enduring reality there is, and takes on its solidity. A soul ruled by wrath leans on what is merely relative, and shares in its fragility. To become more merciful is quite literally to become more — to gather weight and brightness of being — while cruelty is a slow thinning, a drift toward the shadow where a thing is least itself.

etymology: رحمة (mercy): from the root ر-ح-م, the same root as رحم, the womb — a sheltering, life-giving tenderness that enfolds and nourishes what it holds. Mercy is thus not soft sentiment but the enclosing care from which life itself issues, which is why it sits at the innermost heart of the Real rather than at its edge.

وجود (being): from the root و-ج-د, to find or come upon. To exist is to be found as present and there; and a thing is found more fully, stands more firmly in وجود, the nearer it draws to الحق, the source that lends it its very presence.

notes.body:
The picture the passage draws is one mirror, not two. When we stand before an ordinary mirror we see ourself — the very same face — yet turned around, our right hand becoming the reflection's left. Nothing new appears in the glass; the image is us, only reversed.

The divine mirror works the same way, and here is the turn of it: **what we meet in it is not Allah's face but our own true condition**, and that condition is the exact reversal of a quality that belongs to Allah alone. Allah is الغني, the One rich beyond all need, sufficient in Himself. Turn that fullness around, as a mirror turns a face, and what shows on our side of the glass is its opposite — sheer emptiness, total need. We are الفقراء, the utterly poor, and this poverty is the faithful, reversed image of His richness.

> يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ أَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِۖ وَٱللَّهُ هُوَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ

'O mankind, ye are the poor before Allah, and Allah, He is the Rich, the absolutely Praiseworthy'
Fatir 35:15

So to the reader's question: the soul is at once the one gazing and the surface that reflects, but what is reversed is neither Allah's essence nor simply our own shape. **It is a divine attribute crossing over into its created opposite** — His self-sufficiency read backwards becomes our dependence, His transcendence read backwards becomes our nothingness.

This is why the passage speaks of two likenesses at once:

- The right way round — we are merciful because Allah is merciful, and the mercy we give returns to us.
- Reversed — the more truly we grasp His absolute richness, the more clearly we see our own absolute poverty.

To look honestly into the divine mirror is to come away knowing exactly how small we are, and to know, in the same glance, that this smallness is itself the surest trace of His greatness.

etymology: فقر (poverty): from the root ف-ق-ر, which names the vertebrae of the spine (فقرة). A فقير is, quite literally, one whose backbone is broken — bent so low he cannot stand on his own. The word carries far more than lack of money; it means utter dependence, a creature unable to hold itself upright without Allah.

غني (richness): from the root غ-ن-ي, to be free of need, to suffice. الغني is the One who needs nothing beyond Himself and from whom every other thing draws its sufficiency. The same root gives أغنى, to make another rich — self-sufficiency belonging by nature to Allah, borrowed by everything else.

مرآة (mirror): from the root ر-أ-ي, to see, the very root that gives رؤية, vision. A مرآة is literally the instrument of seeing. It adds nothing of its own; it only returns sight — which is exactly why it fits an image about seeing ourselves and, in that seeing, glimpsing Allah reflected.
